tool.name: Lua
tool.tagline: Tiny, fast embeddable scripting language for games, editors and config
tool.description: Lua is a small, fast, dynamically typed scripting language designed to be embedded in larger programs. It is the scripting layer of game engines and platforms like Roblox (Luau), LÖVE and World of Warcraft add-ons, of Neovim, Redis, Nginx/OpenResty and many network devices. Its whole design rests on a few powerful ideas (tables, first-class functions, metatables and coroutines), so it is quick to learn and teaches you a lot about how dynamic languages work.

concepts.name: Running Lua
concepts.summary: Run Lua scripts and the interactive interpreter, print values and write comments.
concepts.why: Every other lesson assumes you can run a snippet and see what it prints.
concepts.body:
Lua ships as a tiny C program. Install it from your package manager (`lua5.4`) or build it from source in seconds. Run `lua` with no arguments for an interactive prompt, or `lua script.lua` to run a file; extra command-line arguments arrive in the global table `arg`.

`print` writes its arguments separated by tabs and ends the line. `io.write` writes without separators or a newline, which is handy when you want full control over output.

- A comment starts with `--` and runs to the end of the line.
- A block comment is `--[[ ... ]]`.
- Semicolons between statements are optional and rarely used.
- Lua is case sensitive: `print` and `Print` are different names.

In many places you will not run Lua directly: it is embedded in a host program (Neovim, Redis, a game engine) that loads your script and exposes its own API. The language is the same everywhere, but the available libraries depend on the host. Standalone Lua gives you the standard library: `string`, `table`, `math`, `io`, `os`, `coroutine` and `utf8`.

LuaJIT and Roblox's Luau are popular dialects based on Lua 5.1; most of what you learn here transfers, but 5.4 features like integer division and `<close>` variables may be missing there.
concepts.code:
-- hello.lua: run with `lua hello.lua a b`
print("Hello, Lua!")          --> Hello, Lua!
print(1, "two", true)         --> 1	two	true
io.write("no newline", "\n")  --> no newline
print(_VERSION)               --> Lua 5.4

--[[ A block comment
     can span lines ]]
print(#arg)                   --> number of script arguments (2 above)
takeaways: `lua file.lua` runs a script; `lua` alone opens a REPL
`--` starts a comment, `--[[ ]]` a block comment
The host program decides which libraries are available
pitfalls: Assuming every host has `io` and `os`: sandboxed embeddings often remove them.

options: An error: print takes one argument
quiz.explain: print accepts any number of arguments and separates them with tabs.

concepts.name: Values, types and variables
concepts.summary: Lua's eight types, integer versus float numbers, and why you should declare variables local.
concepts.why: Knowing the types and the local/global rule prevents the most common Lua bugs.
concepts.body:
Lua is dynamically typed: values have types, variables don't. There are eight types, and `type(v)` returns the name as a string: `nil`, `boolean`, `number`, `string`, `function`, `table`, `thread` (coroutines) and `userdata` (C data).

Since 5.3 a **number** has two subtypes: integers (64-bit) and floats. `3` is an integer and `3.0` a float; `math.type` tells them apart. `/` always gives a float, `//` is floor division and `^` is exponentiation (always a float). Integer arithmetic wraps around on overflow instead of turning into a float.

Strings are immutable byte sequences, written with single quotes, double quotes, or long brackets `[[ ... ]]` for multi-line text. Concatenate with `..`; `#s` is the length in bytes.

Variables are **global by default**. Assigning to an undeclared name creates a global, and reading a misspelled name silently gives `nil`. Always write `local x = 1`: locals are faster, scoped to their block, and cannot leak.

Lua supports multiple assignment, `local a, b = 1, 2`, and swapping with `a, b = b, a`. Extra values are discarded and missing ones become `nil`.
concepts.code:
local n, f = 10, 10.0
print(type(n), math.type(n), math.type(f))  --> number	integer	float
print(n == f)          --> true (same mathematical value)
print(7 / 2, 7 // 2)   --> 3.5	3
print(2 ^ 10)          --> 1024.0
print(math.maxinteger + 1 == math.mininteger) --> true (wraps)

local s = "Lua" .. " " .. 5.4
print(s, #s)           --> Lua 5.4	7

local a, b, c = 1, 2
print(a, b, c)         --> 1	2	nil
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)            --> 2	1

function leak() counter = 1 end  -- oops: creates a global
leak()
print(counter)         --> 1
takeaways: Eight types; `type(v)` returns the name as a string
Numbers are integers or floats; `/` gives a float, `//` floors
Declare everything `local`; undeclared names are globals
pitfalls: A typo in a variable name silently reads `nil` instead of raising an error.

quiz.q: What does 7 // 2 evaluate to in Lua 5.4?
quiz.explain: // is floor division; with two integers it returns the integer 3.

quiz.q: What happens when you assign x = 5 inside a function without local?
options: x is local to the file
x is local to the function
quiz.explain: Undeclared variables are globals in Lua, which is why local should be the default.

concepts.name: Conditions and loops
concepts.summary: if/elseif, while, repeat-until and the numeric for loop, plus Lua's truthiness rule.
concepts.why: Control flow is how every program decides and repeats, and Lua's truthiness differs from many languages.
concepts.body:
Blocks in Lua end with `end`. A conditional is `if cond then ... elseif cond then ... else ... end`.

The truthiness rule is simple: **only `nil` and `false` are falsy**. Zero and the empty string are true, which surprises people coming from Python, JavaScript or C.

The logical operators `and`, `or` and `not` short-circuit and return one of their operands, not a boolean. That gives two idioms: `x = x or default` for defaults, and `cond and a or b` as a ternary (which breaks when `a` is `false` or `nil`).

Comparisons use `==` and `~=` (not equal). Comparing values of different types is always false for `==`, so `1 == "1"` is false.

Loops:

- `while cond do ... end` checks before each iteration.
- `repeat ... until cond` runs at least once; locals declared inside are visible in the `until` condition.
- `for i = start, stop, step do ... end` is the numeric for; the step defaults to 1 and the bounds are evaluated once. The loop variable is local to the loop.

`break` leaves the innermost loop. There is no `continue`; use `goto continue` with a `::continue::` label at the end of the body, or restructure with an `if`.
concepts.code:
local function describe(n)
  if n < 0 then return "negative"
  elseif n == 0 then return "zero"
  else return "positive" end
end
print(describe(-3), describe(0))   --> negative	zero

if 0 then print("0 is true") end   --> 0 is true
local name = nil
print(name or "anonymous")         --> anonymous

for i = 10, 1, -3 do io.write(i, " ") end  --> 10 7 4 1
print()

local i = 0
repeat i = i + 1 until i * i > 20
print(i)                           --> 5

for k = 1, 5 do
  if k % 2 == 0 then goto continue end
  io.write(k, " ")                 --> 1 3 5
  ::continue::
end
print()
takeaways: Only `nil` and `false` are falsy; 0 and "" are true
`x or default` is the default-value idiom
Not-equal is `~=`; there is no `continue`, use `goto continue`
pitfalls: Writing `cond and a or b` when `a` can be false or nil: you always get `b`.

quiz.q: Which values are falsy in Lua?
quiz.explain: Lua treats every value except nil and false as true, including 0 and the empty string.

concepts.name: Tables: arrays and dictionaries
concepts.summary: The table is Lua's only data structure: use it as an array, a dictionary, an object or a module.
concepts.why: Everything nontrivial in Lua is built from tables, so you need them from day one.
concepts.body:
A **table** is an associative array: any value except `nil` (and NaN) can be a key. Lua uses tables for arrays, records, sets, objects, modules and namespaces.

Construct one with braces. Positional values get integer keys starting at **1**, not 0: `{"a", "b"}` has `t[1] == "a"`. Named fields `{x = 1}` are sugar for string keys, and `t.x` is sugar for `t["x"]`. Use brackets for any other key: `{[10] = "ten", ["my key"] = true}`.

Reading a missing key returns `nil`. Assigning `nil` deletes the key.

The length operator `#t` gives the length of the **sequence** part: it is only well defined when the integer keys are 1..n with no `nil` holes. For arrays use `t[#t + 1] = v` or `table.insert(t, v)` to append, `table.remove(t)` to pop, `table.concat` to join strings and `table.sort` to sort in place.

Tables are reference values: assigning a table to another variable doesn't copy it, and two tables are `==` only if they are the same table. That makes them cheap to pass around, but you need to copy explicitly when you want an independent value.
concepts.code:
local fruits = {"apple", "banana"}
fruits[#fruits + 1] = "cherry"
table.insert(fruits, 1, "kiwi")        -- insert at position 1
print(#fruits, fruits[1])              --> 4	kiwi
print(table.concat(fruits, ", "))      --> kiwi, apple, banana, cherry

local point = {x = 3, y = 4, ["z-axis"] = 0}
point.x = nil                          -- delete a key
print(point.x, point["z-axis"])        --> nil	0

local alias = fruits
alias[1] = "lime"
print(fruits[1])                       --> lime (same table)
print({} == {})                        --> false

table.sort(fruits)
print(table.concat(fruits, " "))       --> apple banana cherry lime
print(table.remove(fruits), #fruits)   --> lime	3
takeaways: Tables are the only data structure: arrays, maps, objects, modules
Arrays start at index 1; `t.x` means `t["x"]`
`#t` is reliable only for sequences without nil holes
Tables are references, compared by identity
pitfalls: Storing nil in the middle of an array, which makes `#t` and ipairs unreliable.

quiz.explain: Array-style constructors start at index 1, so key 0 was never set and reading it returns nil.

quiz.q: What does local b = a do when a is a table?
options: Makes b refer to the same table
quiz.explain: Tables are reference values, so both names point to the same table.

concepts.name: Functions and multiple returns
concepts.summary: Define functions, return several values, accept variable arguments and pass functions around.
concepts.why: Functions are first-class values in Lua and the main tool for structuring code.
concepts.body:
`function add(a, b) return a + b end` is sugar for assigning a function value to a variable; prefer `local function add(a, b) ... end` so it doesn't become a global. Functions are values: store them in tables, pass them as arguments, return them.

Arguments are positional. Missing arguments are `nil` and extra ones are dropped, so `a = a or 1` is the usual way to give a default.

A function can **return multiple values**: `return q, r`. The caller receives as many as it asks for. The adjustment rule matters: a call returns all its values only when it is the last expression in a list. In the middle, or wrapped in parentheses, it is cut to one value.

Variadic functions use `...`. Inside, `select("#", ...)` counts the arguments (including nils) and `{...}` or `table.pack(...)` collects them; `table.unpack(t)` does the reverse, spreading a table into arguments.

When a function takes a single table or string literal, you can drop the parentheses: `f{x = 1}` and `print "hi"`. The table form is a common way to fake named arguments.

Lua performs proper **tail calls**: `return f(x)` reuses the stack frame, so tail-recursive loops never overflow.
concepts.code:
local function divmod(a, b)
  return a // b, a % b
end
local q, r = divmod(17, 5)
print(q, r)                    --> 3	2
print(divmod(17, 5), "end")    --> 3	end (cut to one value)
print((divmod(17, 5)))         --> 3

local function sum(...)
  local total = 0
  for _, v in ipairs({...}) do total = total + v end
  return total, select("#", ...)
end
print(sum(1, 2, 3))            --> 6	3
print(sum(table.unpack({4, 5}))) --> 9	2

local function greet(opts)
  local name = opts.name or "world"
  return "hello " .. name
end
print(greet{name = "Ana"})     --> hello Ana
takeaways: Use `local function` so functions don't become globals
A call expands to all its results only as the last item in a list
`...`, `select("#", ...)` and `table.unpack` handle varargs
`f{...}` with a table fakes named arguments
pitfalls: Expecting `f(), x` to keep all of f's return values; only the last call expands.

quiz.q: local function two() return 1, 2 end. What does print(two(), 9) print?
quiz.explain: two() isn't the last expression, so it is adjusted to its first result.

concepts.name: Strings and patterns
concepts.summary: Format, search and transform text with the string library and Lua patterns.
concepts.why: Text processing is a daily task, and Lua patterns look like regex but behave differently.
concepts.body:
All string functions live in the `string` table, and strings have it as their metatable, so `s:upper()` is the same as `string.upper(s)`. The colon passes `s` as the first argument.

Indexes are 1-based and negative indexes count from the end: `s:sub(-3)` is the last three bytes. `string.format` works like C's printf (`%d`, `%5.2f`, `%s`, `%q` for a quoted literal). `s:rep(n)`, `s:reverse()` and `s:byte()`/`string.char` round out the basics.

**Patterns** are Lua's lightweight alternative to regular expressions. Classes are written with `%`: `%d` digit, `%a` letter, `%s` space, `%w` alphanumeric, and the uppercase version negates. Quantifiers are `*`, `+`, `?` and `-` (lazy `*`). Captures use parentheses. There is no alternation (`|`) and no `{n,m}`.

- `s:find(p)` returns the start and end index, plus captures.
- `s:match(p)` returns the captures (or the whole match).
- `s:gmatch(p)` iterates over all matches in a `for` loop.
- `s:gsub(p, repl)` replaces; `repl` can be a string with `%1`, a table or a function.

Because `%` escapes magic characters, write `%.` for a literal dot. Pass `true` as the fourth argument of `find` for a plain substring search.

Strings are bytes: for UTF-8 text use the `utf8` library (`utf8.len`, `utf8.codes`).
concepts.code:
local s = "Lua 5.4 was released in 2020"
print(s:upper():sub(1, 3))           --> LUA
print(s:find("%d+"))                 --> 5	5
print(s:match("(%d+)%.(%d+)"))       --> 5	4

for word in s:gmatch("%a+") do io.write(word, ",") end
print()                              --> Lua,was,released,in,

local out, n = s:gsub("%d+", function(d) return "<" .. d .. ">" end)
print(out, n)  --> Lua <5>.<4> was released in <2020>	3

print(("key = value"):match("^(%w+)%s*=%s*(%w+)$"))  --> key	value
print(string.format("%-5s|%6.2f|%q", "ab", math.pi, "hi")) --> ab   |  3.14|"hi"
print(#"héllo", utf8.len("héllo"))   --> 6	5
takeaways: `s:method()` calls `string.method(s)`
Patterns use `%` classes (`%d`, `%a`, `%s`) and have no alternation
`gsub` accepts a string, table or function as the replacement
Use `utf8` functions for character counts in UTF-8 text
pitfalls: Using `.` or `-` unescaped when you mean the literal character; write `%.` and `%-`.

quiz.q: What does ("a.b.c"):gsub(".", "-") return as its first value?
quiz.explain: An unescaped . matches any character, so all five characters are replaced; use %. for a literal dot.

concepts.name: Iterators: pairs, ipairs and generic for
concepts.summary: Loop over tables with pairs and ipairs, and write your own iterator functions.
concepts.why: The generic for is how you traverse every table and stream in Lua.
concepts.body:
The **generic for** loop, `for k, v in explist do ... end`, calls an iterator function repeatedly until it returns `nil`.

- `ipairs(t)` walks `t[1]`, `t[2]`, ... in order and stops at the first `nil`. Use it for arrays.
- `pairs(t)` visits every key in the table, in an **unspecified order**. Use it for dictionaries, and never rely on the order. To iterate in a fixed order, collect the keys, `table.sort` them, then loop.

You must not add new keys to a table while traversing it with `pairs` (assigning to existing fields, including setting them to `nil`, is allowed).

Writing your own iterator is easy with a closure: return a function that produces the next value each call and `nil` when done. Under the hood the generic for accepts three values (an iterator function, an invariant state and a control value), which is how `pairs` and `ipairs` avoid allocating closures. Lua 5.4 adds a fourth closing value used with to-be-closed variables.

Iterators make lazy pipelines natural: `io.lines(path)` returns an iterator over a file's lines and `s:gmatch` one over pattern matches, so you can process large inputs without building a table first.
concepts.code:
local scores = {ana = 90, bo = 72, cy = 85}

local names = {}
for name in pairs(scores) do names[#names + 1] = name end
table.sort(names)                      -- fixed order
for i, name in ipairs(names) do
  print(i, name, scores[name])
end
--> 1	ana	90
--> 2	bo	72
--> 3	cy	85

local function range(n, step)
  local i = 0
  return function()                    -- closure iterator
    i = i + (step or 1)
    if i <= n then return i end
  end
end
for x in range(10, 4) do io.write(x, " ") end  --> 4 8
print()

for i, v in ipairs({1, 2, nil, 4}) do io.write(v, " ") end --> 1 2
print()
takeaways: `ipairs` for arrays (stops at the first nil), `pairs` for all keys
`pairs` order is unspecified; sort keys when order matters
An iterator is just a function that returns nil when finished
pitfalls: Adding keys to a table while iterating it with pairs, which is undefined behaviour.

quiz.q: for i, v in ipairs({1, 2, nil, 4}) prints how many elements?
quiz.explain: ipairs stops at the first nil, so only 1 and 2 are visited.

concepts.name: Closures and upvalues
concepts.summary: Functions capture the local variables around them, giving you private state without classes.
concepts.why: Closures power callbacks, iterators, memoisation and simple objects throughout Lua code.
concepts.body:
Lua has **lexical scoping**: a function can read and write the local variables of the blocks that enclose it, even after those blocks have finished. A captured variable is called an **upvalue**.

Each time a `function` expression is evaluated, a new closure is created with its own references to the captured variables. Two closures created in the same call share the same upvalue, so they see each other's updates.

This gives you private state cheaply. A counter factory returns a function that increments a local; nobody outside can touch the count. Memoisation is a closure over a cache table. Callbacks passed to an event system capture the context they need.

Loops create a fresh local for each iteration: closures created inside `for i = 1, 3` each capture their own `i`, unlike `var` in old JavaScript.

Scope rules worth remembering:

- A `local` is visible from the statement after its declaration to the end of its block.
- `local function f` makes `f` visible inside its own body, so it can recurse; `local f = function` does not.
- `do ... end` creates a block purely to limit scope.

Accessing upvalues is slightly slower than locals but much faster than globals, which is why performance-sensitive code often caches globals in locals (`local insert = table.insert`).
concepts.code:
local function counter()
  local n = 0
  return function() n = n + 1; return n end,
         function() return n end
end
local inc, get = counter()
inc(); inc()
print(get())                 --> 2 (shared upvalue)

local fns = {}
for i = 1, 3 do fns[i] = function() return i end end
print(fns[1](), fns[3]())    --> 1	3 (fresh i per iteration)

local function memoize(f)
  local cache = {}
  return function(x)
    local v = cache[x]
    if v == nil then v = f(x); cache[x] = v end
    return v
  end
end
local slow_sq = memoize(function(x) print("computing", x); return x * x end)
print(slow_sq(4))            --> computing	4 / 16
print(slow_sq(4))            --> 16 (cached)
takeaways: A closure captures enclosing locals (upvalues) by reference
Closures created in one call share the same upvalues
Each loop iteration gets a fresh loop variable
pitfalls: Using `local f = function() ... f() ... end` for recursion: inside the body `f` is still the global (nil).

quiz.q: Two closures returned from the same call to counter() both use n. What happens when one increments it?
options: The other sees the new value
Only the first call is affected
quiz.explain: Closures created in the same activation share the upvalue, so changes are visible to both.

concepts.name: Modules and require
concepts.summary: Split code into files that return a table, and load them with require.
concepts.why: Every real Lua project and every host (Neovim, LÖVE) organises code as modules.
concepts.body:
A **module** is just a file that returns a value, almost always a table of functions. Keep the implementation `local` and export only what you put in the table.

`require("mylib.util")` turns the dots into directory separators and searches the templates in `package.path` (for Lua files, e.g. `./?.lua;./?/init.lua;...`) and `package.cpath` (for C libraries). The loaded result is cached in `package.loaded`, so the file runs **once** no matter how many times it is required, and every caller shares the same table.

Conventions:

- Return a table; don't set globals from a module.
- Name the local table `M` (or the module name) and `return M` at the end.
- `require` passes the module name as `...` to the chunk, useful for requiring siblings.

To reload during development set `package.loaded[name] = nil` and require again. Hosts usually add their own search paths: Neovim looks under `lua/` in each runtime directory, and LuaRocks, Lua's package manager, installs libraries into a tree that it adds to the paths.

Lower level, `load(str)` compiles a string into a function and `dofile`/`loadfile` do the same for files without caching.
concepts.code:
-- Simulate a file mathx.lua via package.preload
package.preload["mathx"] = function(name)
  local M = {}
  local function check(n) assert(type(n) == "number", "number expected") end
  function M.clamp(x, lo, hi)
    check(x)
    return math.max(lo, math.min(hi, x))
  end
  print("loading " .. name)
  return M
end

local mx = require("mathx")      --> loading mathx
local again = require("mathx")   -- cached: prints nothing
print(mx == again)               --> true
print(mx.clamp(15, 0, 10))       --> 10
print(mx.check)                  --> nil (private)
print(package.path ~= nil)       --> true

local f = load("return 2 + 3")
print(f())                       --> 5
takeaways: A module is a file that returns a table
`require` runs a module once and caches it in `package.loaded`
Keep helpers `local`; export only through the returned table
pitfalls: Setting globals from a module, which leaks names into every other module.

quiz.q: A module file is required from three different files. How many times does its top-level code run?
quiz.explain: require caches the result in package.loaded and returns the cached value afterwards.

concepts.name: Errors, pcall and assert
concepts.summary: Raise errors with error and assert, and catch them with pcall and xpcall.
concepts.why: Lua has no try/catch; knowing pcall is essential for robust scripts and plugins.
concepts.body:
`error(msg)` raises an error. The message can be any value, including a table carrying structured data. With a string, Lua prepends the position (`file:line:`); pass a level as the second argument to blame the caller (`error(msg, 2)`) or `0` to add nothing.

`assert(v, msg)` raises `msg` when `v` is falsy and otherwise returns all its arguments, so `local f = assert(io.open(path))` is idiomatic: `io.open` returns `nil, message` on failure and `assert` turns that into an error.

To catch errors call the function through `pcall` (protected call): `local ok, result = pcall(f, arg1, arg2)`. On success `ok` is `true` followed by f's results; on failure `ok` is `false` and the second value is the error object. `xpcall(f, handler, ...)` also calls a message handler before the stack unwinds, which is where you grab `debug.traceback`.

Two error styles coexist in Lua code:

- Return `nil, errmsg` for expected failures (file not found, bad input). The standard library does this.
- Raise with `error` for bugs and unrecoverable situations.

For cleanup, Lua 5.4 adds to-be-closed variables: `local f <close> = obj` calls the value's `__close` metamethod when the block exits, normally or by error.
concepts.code:
local function parse_age(s)
  local n = tonumber(s)
  if not n then error({code = "EINVAL", input = s}) end
  if n < 0 then error("age must be >= 0", 2) end
  return n
end

local ok, err = pcall(parse_age, "abc")
print(ok, type(err), err.code)         --> false	table	EINVAL

ok, err = pcall(parse_age, "42")
print(ok, err)                         --> true	42

local f, msg = io.open("/no/such/file")
print(f, msg ~= nil)                   --> nil	true

ok, err = xpcall(function() local t = nil; return t.x end,
                 function(e) return "handled: " .. e end)
print(ok, err:match("attempt to index") ~= nil)  --> false	true
takeaways: `pcall(f, ...)` returns `true, results` or `false, err`
`assert(v, msg)` passes values through or raises
Expected failures return `nil, msg`; bugs raise with `error`
pitfalls: Calling `pcall(f(x))`: that calls f outside the protection; write `pcall(f, x)`.

quiz.q: Which call protects f against errors when passing it the argument x?
quiz.explain: pcall must call f itself; f(x) would run before pcall gets control.

concepts.name: Metatables and metamethods
concepts.summary: Customise how tables behave for indexing, arithmetic, comparison, calling and printing.
concepts.why: Metatables are the mechanism behind classes, proxies, default values and operator overloading in Lua.
concepts.body:
Every table can have a **metatable**: an ordinary table whose specially named fields, **metamethods**, define what happens when an operation isn't handled normally. Set it with `setmetatable(t, mt)` (which returns `t`) and read it with `getmetatable(t)`.

The most important ones:

- `__index` runs when a key is **missing**. If it is a table, Lua looks the key up there (and in that table's `__index`, and so on); if it is a function it is called with `(t, key)`. This is how defaults and inheritance work.
- `__newindex` runs when assigning to a missing key; use `rawset` inside it to actually store.
- `__add`, `__sub`, `__mul`, `__eq`, `__lt`, `__le`, `__concat`, `__unm`, `__len` overload operators.
- `__call` makes a table callable; `__tostring` controls `tostring` and `print`; `__close` and `__gc` handle cleanup.

`rawget`, `rawset`, `rawequal` and `rawlen` bypass metamethods, which you need inside them to avoid infinite recursion.

Strings share one metatable whose `__index` is the `string` table, which is why `s:upper()` works. Only tables (and full userdata from C) can have individual metatables set from Lua.

Metamethods are looked up with raw access in the metatable, so they must be present when the operation happens; adding `__gc` after `setmetatable` doesn't register it.
concepts.code:
local Vec = {}
Vec.__index = Vec
local function vec(x, y) return setmetatable({x = x, y = y}, Vec) end

Vec.__add = function(a, b) return vec(a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y) end
Vec.__eq = function(a, b) return a.x == b.x and a.y == b.y end
Vec.__tostring = function(v) return "(" .. v.x .. ", " .. v.y .. ")" end
function Vec.len(v) return math.sqrt(v.x ^ 2 + v.y ^ 2) end

local a = vec(3, 4)
print(tostring(a + vec(1, 1)))   --> (4, 5)
print(a == vec(3, 4))            --> true
print(a:len())                   --> 5.0 (found through __index)

local defaults = setmetatable({}, {__index = function(t, k) return 0 end})
defaults.hits = defaults.hits + 1
print(defaults.hits, defaults.misses)   --> 1	0

local readonly = setmetatable({}, {__newindex = function() error("read-only", 2) end})
print(pcall(function() readonly.x = 1 end))  --> false	...read-only
takeaways: `__index` handles missing keys: a table to delegate, a function to compute
Arithmetic, comparison, call and tostring are all overridable
Use `rawget`/`rawset` inside metamethods to avoid recursion
pitfalls: Expecting `__index` to run for keys that exist: it only fires on missing keys.

quiz.q: When does a table's __index metamethod run?
options: When reading a key that is absent from the table
Only when calling a method with :
quiz.explain: __index is a fallback for lookups that find nil in the table itself.

options: It is required for numeric keys
quiz.explain: The key is still missing, so a normal assignment would recurse into __newindex forever.

concepts.name: Classes and inheritance with metatables
concepts.summary: Build classes, methods and single inheritance from tables, __index and the colon syntax.
concepts.why: Most Lua codebases (games, plugins, libraries) use this pattern for objects.
concepts.body:
Lua has no class keyword. Instead a **class** is a table of methods, and instances are tables whose metatable has `__index` pointing at that class. Missing fields (the methods) are found on the class.

The **colon syntax** wires up `self`. `function Account:deposit(v)` defines a function with a hidden first parameter `self`, and `acc:deposit(10)` calls `Account.deposit(acc, 10)`. Mixing `.` and `:` is the classic bug: `acc.deposit(10)` passes 10 as `self`.

A typical constructor is `function Class.new(...)` that creates a table, sets the metatable and initialises fields. Setting `Class.__index = Class` lets the class serve as its own metatable.

**Inheritance** chains lookups: make the subclass's metatable index the parent class (`setmetatable(Sub, {__index = Base})`). A missing method is searched in the instance, then the subclass, then the base. Call the parent's method explicitly with `Base.method(self, ...)`; there is no `super`.

Privacy is a convention (an underscore prefix) unless you use closures instead of tables for state. Many projects use a small class library (middleclass, classic), but they are thin wrappers over exactly this mechanism, so it pays to understand it directly.
concepts.code:
local Account = {}
Account.__index = Account

function Account.new(owner, balance)
  return setmetatable({owner = owner, balance = balance or 0}, Account)
end
function Account:deposit(v) self.balance = self.balance + v end
function Account:describe() return self.owner .. ": " .. self.balance end

local Savings = setmetatable({}, {__index = Account})
Savings.__index = Savings
function Savings.new(owner, balance, rate)
  local self = Account.new(owner, balance)
  self.rate = rate
  return setmetatable(self, Savings)
end
function Savings:add_interest() self:deposit(self.balance * self.rate) end
function Savings:describe()
  return Account.describe(self) .. " @" .. self.rate   -- call "super"
end

local s = Savings.new("ana", 100, 0.05)
s:add_interest()
print(s:describe())                --> ana: 105.0 @0.05
print(getmetatable(s) == Savings)  --> true
takeaways: A class is a method table used as the instances' `__index`
`obj:m(x)` is `obj.m(obj, x)`; define methods with `:` to get `self`
Inheritance = the subclass table's own `__index` points at the base
pitfalls: Calling a method with a dot (`obj.m()`), so `self` is missing or wrong.

quiz.explain: The colon call passes the receiver as the first argument, which becomes self.

concepts.name: Coroutines
concepts.summary: Suspend and resume functions with coroutine.yield and resume to write generators and cooperative tasks.
concepts.why: Coroutines drive game scripting, async I/O in OpenResty and Neovim, and elegant generators.
concepts.body:
A **coroutine** is a function with its own stack that can pause itself and be resumed later. It is cooperative: only one runs at a time, and it runs until it explicitly yields.

- `coroutine.create(f)` makes a coroutine (type `thread`) without running it.
- `coroutine.resume(co, ...)` starts or continues it. It returns `true` plus the values passed to `yield` (or returned at the end), or `false, err` if the coroutine raised an error.
- `coroutine.yield(...)` suspends the current coroutine; the values become resume's results, and the arguments of the next `resume` become yield's return values.
- `coroutine.status(co)` is `suspended`, `running`, `normal` or `dead`.
- `coroutine.wrap(f)` returns a function that resumes on each call and re-raises errors, perfect for **generators** used in a generic for.

Because the stack is preserved, a coroutine can yield from deep inside nested calls. That lets you write sequential-looking code (wait for an animation, then for input, then for a timer) while a scheduler resumes the coroutine when each event happens. OpenResty and many Neovim plugins turn callback APIs into straight-line code exactly this way.

`coroutine.close(co)` (5.4) kills a suspended coroutine and runs its pending to-be-closed variables. Yielding across a C call boundary only works when the C function supports continuations.
concepts.code:
local function numbers(limit)
  return coroutine.wrap(function()
    for i = 1, limit do coroutine.yield(i, i * i) end
  end)
end
for n, sq in numbers(3) do io.write(n, ":", sq, " ") end
print()                               --> 1:1 2:4 3:9

local co = coroutine.create(function(a)
  print("got", a)                     --> got	1
  local b = coroutine.yield(a + 1)
  print("got", b)                     --> got	10
  return "done"
end)
print(coroutine.resume(co, 1))        --> true	2
print(coroutine.status(co))           --> suspended
print(coroutine.resume(co, 10))       --> true	done
print(coroutine.status(co))           --> dead
print(coroutine.resume(co))           --> false	cannot resume dead coroutine
takeaways: `resume` passes values in; `yield` passes values out, and vice versa
`coroutine.wrap` gives a function, ideal for generators
Coroutines are cooperative and keep their whole call stack
pitfalls: Ignoring resume's first return value: errors inside a coroutine are returned, not raised.

quiz.q: A coroutine raises an error. What does coroutine.resume return?
quiz.explain: resume works like pcall: errors come back as false plus the error object (wrap re-raises instead).

concepts.name: Garbage collection and weak tables
concepts.summary: How Lua's incremental and generational collectors work, and how weak tables and __gc interact with them.
concepts.why: Long-running hosts (games, servers, editors) depend on predictable memory and leak-free caches.
concepts.body:
Lua manages memory with a tracing garbage collector. Lua 5.4 offers two modes, switched with `collectgarbage("incremental")` or `collectgarbage("generational")`.

- **Incremental** (the library default) is a tri-colour mark-and-sweep that interleaves small steps with your program, so pauses stay short. The pause parameter controls how much memory grows before a new cycle starts; the step multiplier controls how much work each step does.
- **Generational** collects young objects often and old ones rarely, which suits programs that create many short-lived tables. The standalone `lua` interpreter switches to this mode at startup.

`collectgarbage("count")` reports the heap in KB, `collectgarbage()` forces a full cycle and `"step"` does a bit of work.

A table with a metatable field `__mode` is **weak**: `"k"` makes keys weak, `"v"` values, `"kv"` both. A weak reference doesn't keep an object alive, so entries vanish when the object is otherwise unreachable. Use weak keys to attach data to objects you don't own and weak values for caches. Strings and numbers are values, not collectable objects, so they are never removed from weak tables. Ephemeron semantics mean a weak-key entry whose value refers back to its key is still collected.

`__gc` on a table's metatable registers a **finalizer**, called once before the object is collected. Finalizers run in reverse order of marking, may resurrect objects, and must be set when `setmetatable` is called. Prefer `<close>` for deterministic cleanup.
concepts.code:
local cache = setmetatable({}, {__mode = "k"})  -- weak keys

local obj = {}
cache[obj] = "metadata"
local n = 0
for _ in pairs(cache) do n = n + 1 end
print(n)                                 --> 1

obj = nil                                -- drop the only strong ref
collectgarbage()
n = 0
for _ in pairs(cache) do n = n + 1 end
print(n)                                 --> 0

local before = collectgarbage("count")
local junk = {}
for i = 1, 1e5 do junk[i] = {i} end
junk = nil
collectgarbage()
print(collectgarbage("count") < before + 100)  --> true

setmetatable({}, {__gc = function() print("finalized") end})
collectgarbage()                         --> finalized
print(collectgarbage("incremental"))     --> generational (previous mode, standalone lua)
takeaways: Two collectors: incremental (library default) and generational
`__mode = "k"`/`"v"` makes weak tables for caches and side data
`__gc` finalizers run once before collection; prefer `<close>` for timely cleanup
pitfalls: Expecting string keys in a weak-key table to disappear; strings are not collectable references.

quiz.q: You want a cache that doesn't keep its cached objects alive. Which metatable do you use?
quiz.explain: Weak values let the collector remove entries whose values are no longer referenced elsewhere.

concepts.name: Embedding Lua: the C API
concepts.summary: Embed the interpreter in a C program and expose C functions through Lua's virtual stack.
concepts.why: Embedding is Lua's core purpose: every host from Redis to game engines uses this API.
concepts.body:
Lua is a C library first. A host creates an interpreter with `luaL_newstate()`, opens the standard libraries with `luaL_openlibs`, runs code with `luaL_dostring` or `luaL_loadfile` plus `lua_pcall`, and destroys it with `lua_close`. Each `lua_State` is fully independent, so a host can run many sandboxes.

All data exchange goes through a **virtual stack**. You push values (`lua_pushinteger`, `lua_pushstring`), read them by index (`lua_tointeger(L, -1)`; positive indexes count from the bottom, negative from the top) and pop them with `lua_pop`. Lua's garbage collector owns the values; the stack protects them from being collected while you use them.

A C function callable from Lua has the signature `int f(lua_State *L)`: it reads its arguments from the stack (`luaL_checkinteger(L, 1)` validates and raises a Lua error on bad input), pushes its results and returns how many it pushed. Register it with `lua_register` or, for a module, a `luaL_Reg` array and `luaL_newlib` inside a `luaopen_name` function that `require` finds via `package.cpath`.

Lua errors use `longjmp`, so a C function that raises never returns; always run Lua code with `lua_pcall` at the top level. Keep references to Lua values beyond a call in the registry (`luaL_ref`), and use full userdata with a metatable to wrap C structs.
takeaways: All values cross between C and Lua via the virtual stack
A C function returns the number of results it pushed
Run Lua code with `lua_pcall`/`luaL_dostring`; errors longjmp
pitfalls: Leaving values on the stack in loops, which grows it until it overflows.

quiz.q: A C function pushes two values and returns 1. What does Lua receive?
quiz.explain: The return count tells Lua how many values from the top of the stack are results.

concepts.name: Performance and table internals
concepts.summary: How tables store array and hash parts, why locals are fast, and the habits that make Lua code quick.
concepts.why: Hot loops in games and servers need code that works with the VM, not against it.
concepts.body:
Internally a table has two parts: an **array part** for integer keys 1..n and a **hash part** for everything else. The array part is sized to the largest n such that more than half of the slots 1..n are in use. Growing a table triggers a **rehash** that recounts keys and reallocates, so building a big table one key at a time costs several reallocations; a constructor with all elements (`{a, b, c}`) sizes it once.

The Lua VM is register-based: **locals live in registers** and are the fastest variables. Upvalues are close behind. Globals are lookups in the `_ENV` table, and `math.floor` is two table lookups, which is why hot code caches them: `local floor = math.floor`.

Strings are interned (short ones, up to 40 bytes) and immutable. Building a string with `s = s .. x` in a loop is quadratic because each step copies; collect pieces in a table and call `table.concat` once.

Other habits:

- Reuse tables instead of allocating in inner loops to reduce GC pressure.
- `#t` on a proper sequence is cheap (a binary search at worst).
- Measure with `os.clock()` before optimising; intuition is often wrong.

**LuaJIT** traces hot loops into machine code and can be many times faster, but it implements Lua 5.1 (plus some 5.2 features), so code must avoid 5.3+ features like integer subtypes and the `//` operator.
concepts.code:
local N = 200000

local t0 = os.clock()
local s = ""
for i = 1, 20000 do s = s .. "x" end      -- quadratic copying
local slow = os.clock() - t0

t0 = os.clock()
local parts = {}
for i = 1, 20000 do parts[i] = "x" end
local s2 = table.concat(parts)            -- one allocation
local fast = os.clock() - t0
print(s == s2, slow > fast)               --> true	true (usually)

local function sum_global() local x = 0
  for i = 1, N do x = x + math.sqrt(i) end return x end
local sqrt = math.sqrt
local function sum_local() local x = 0
  for i = 1, N do x = x + sqrt(i) end return x end

t0 = os.clock(); sum_global(); local g = os.clock() - t0
t0 = os.clock(); sum_local(); local l = os.clock() - t0
print(string.format("global %.4fs, local %.4fs", g, l))
takeaways: Tables have an array part and a hash part; rehash happens on growth
Locals are registers: cache globals in locals in hot loops
Build strings with `table.concat`, not repeated `..`
pitfalls: Optimising without measuring; use `os.clock()` or a profiler first.

quiz.q: Why is building a long string with s = s .. piece inside a loop slow?
options: Each concatenation copies the whole string so far
quiz.explain: Strings are immutable, so every step allocates and copies a new, longer string: quadratic work.
